books.section: Topic 3.6 The Influence of Revolutionary Ideals

primary_sources: Phillis Wheatley, “On Being Brought from Africa to America” (1773)

stimulus.text:
Phillis Wheatley, “On Being Brought from Africa to America,” 1773:

“’Twas mercy brought me from my Pagan land,
Taught my benighted soul to understand
That there’s a God, that there’s a Saviour too:
Once I redemption neither sought nor knew.
Some view our sable race with scornful eye,
‘Their colour is a diabolic die.’
Remember, Christians, Negroes, black as Cain,
May be refin’d, and join th’ angelic train.”
stimulus.source: Phillis Wheatley, “On Being Brought from Africa to America” (1773). Public domain.
stimulus.source_note: Phillis Wheatley, “On Being Brought from Africa to America” (1773). Public domain.

parts.prompt: Identify ONE idea in the poem about Wheatley’s own identity.
parts.modelAnswer: Wheatley presents herself as a Christian convert whose soul was taught to understand God after she was brought from Africa. She describes herself as once not seeking redemption, and now able to join the angelic train.

scoring.criterion: Identifies one idea in the poem about Wheatley’s identity, such as her Christian conversion, her African origin, or her hope of joining the angels.
scoring.notEarned: Describing the poem’s subject without naming an idea about Wheatley herself does not earn the point.

parts.prompt: Explain ONE way the poem challenges ideas about enslaved Africans.
parts.modelAnswer: The poem answers those who call Black skin a diabolic die by saying that Black people, like white Christians, may be refined and join the angels. It claims spiritual equality for Black people at a time when slavery treated them as lesser beings.

scoring.criterion: Explains one way the poem challenges ideas about enslaved Africans, such as claiming their spiritual equality or answering the claim that Black skin marks evil.
scoring.notEarned: Saying only that Wheatley wrote a poem, with no challenge named, does not earn the point.

parts.prompt: Explain ONE limit of the poem as evidence about the lives of enslaved people.
parts.modelAnswer: The poem speaks of Wheatley’s own faith and learning, not of the daily work, punishment, or family separation that most enslaved people endured. Wheatley lived in a Boston household and learned to read and write, so her experience was unlike that of most enslaved people in the colonies.

scoring.criterion: Explains one limit of the poem as evidence, such as that it describes one woman’s faith rather than the daily lives of most enslaved people, or that Wheatley’s household life was unusual.
scoring.notEarned: Saying only that one poem cannot show everything, with no specific limit, does not earn the point.
